tips.title: Penetration and ionising power run opposite
tips.body: **Alpha** is the **most ionising** and the **least penetrating**; **gamma** is the **least ionising** and the **most penetrating**. One rule gives you both columns, because the reason is the same: alpha loses its energy quickly by ionising, so it does not get far.

tips.title: Half-life: count the halvings
tips.body: Divide the time elapsed by the half-life to get the **number of halvings**, then halve that many times. 6 hours at a 2-hour half-life is **3** halvings: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100.

tips.title: Irradiated objects do not become radioactive
tips.body: The specification says it plainly: **the irradiated object does not become radioactive**. Contamination is different — the radioactive **atoms are on the object**, so it keeps emitting until they are removed.

tips.title: Balance the numbers, do not name the element
tips.body: Nuclear equations are **limited to balancing the atomic numbers and mass numbers**. The specification says **identification of daughter elements is not required**, so you never need a periodic table for this.

tips.title: Fission splits, fusion joins
tips.body: **Fission** is the **splitting** of a **large, unstable** nucleus. **Fusion** is the **joining** of two **light** nuclei. The words tell you: fission like *fissure*, a split; fusion like *fuse together*.

why.matters:
Some nuclei are unstable and, at a moment nobody can predict, spit out a piece of themselves to become more stable. That is all radioactivity is. The topic gives you the three things it can spit out, how far each gets and what it does on the way, and the one rule that makes the randomness useful: whatever a sample's size, the time for half of it to go is fixed.

That rule dates bones, times a hospital scan, and sets how long waste must be kept.

examples.title: The alpha source in the smoke alarm
examples.body:
The smoke alarm on the ceiling holds a tiny **alpha** source. Alpha is the most ionising radiation, so in a small open chamber it turns the air into ions and a minute current flows between two plates. Smoke drifting in absorbs the alpha particles before they can ionise the air, the current drops, and the alarm sounds.

Alpha is the right choice for the same reason it is dangerous inside the body: it does a great deal to the first few centimetres of anything it meets, and then it is stopped. The alarm's plastic case stops it completely, so the source is harmless on the ceiling.

boxes.title: Most ionising
boxes.body: Alpha turns the air in the chamber into ions, so a small current flows.

boxes.title: Smoke stops it
boxes.body: Smoke absorbs the alpha before it reaches the air. The current falls; the alarm sounds.

boxes.title: Shortest range
boxes.body: A few centimetres of air, or the plastic case, stops it completely.

boxes.title: So it is safe
boxes.body: Nothing gets out of the alarm. Only the smoke that gets in changes anything.

visual.alt: Four boxes explaining why a smoke alarm uses an alpha source: alpha ionises the air in the chamber to give a current, smoke absorbs it and the current falls, and alpha's short range means the case stops it entirely

examples.title: Why a hospital tracer is gone by the weekend
examples.body:
A patient having an organ scanned is given a **gamma** emitter with a half-life of about 6 hours. Gamma, because it has to get out of the body to the detector. Six hours, because the dose should not last.

Half-life does the rest of the arithmetic. After 6 hours half the tracer is left; after 24 hours, 4 half-lives, a sixteenth; after 60 hours, 10 half-lives, about a thousandth. The scan happens in the first hour, the patient is essentially clear by the next day, and the hospital's own bins of used tracer only need holding for a few days before they are ordinary waste.

examples.title: How a bone is dated
examples.body:
Living things take in carbon all their lives, and a tiny fixed fraction of it is **carbon-14**, an unstable isotope with a half-life of 5 730 years. Death stops the intake, and from then on the carbon-14 only decays. Its half-life becomes a clock.

Measure the fraction of carbon-14 left in a bone against living wood. Half means one half-life, 5 730 years. A quarter means two, 11 460 years. An eighth means 17 190. The clock cannot be reset, hurried or slowed, because decay is random and nothing done to the sample changes its rate, which is the same fact the lesson makes about randomness, used.

visual.alt: A table dating a bone by its carbon fourteen: half left is one half-life of five thousand seven hundred and thirty years, a quarter is two, an eighth is three at just over seventeen thousand years

steps.title: Radioactive decay
steps.body:
**Some atomic nuclei are unstable.** Such a nucleus **gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable**. This is **a random process called radioactive decay**.

**Random** is a precise claim, and it is examined. It means you **cannot predict when any individual nucleus will decay**, and nothing you do to the sample — heating it, compressing it, reacting it chemically — changes the rate. All that can be said is the **probability** of decay in a given time, which is why large numbers behave predictably while single nuclei do not.

**Two measurements, and they are not the same thing:**

**Activity** is **the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays**, measured in **becquerel (Bq)**. One becquerel is one decay per second.

**Count-rate** is **the number of decays recorded each second by a detector**, such as a **Geiger-Muller tube**.

**The difference matters.** A detector only catches the radiation that happens to travel into it, so the **count-rate is always lower than the activity**. Move the detector further away and the count-rate falls even though the activity has not changed at all.

**The nuclear radiation emitted may be** an **alpha particle (α)**, a **beta particle (β)**, a **gamma ray (γ)**, or a **neutron (n)**.

steps.title: The three radiations
steps.body:
**Alpha (α)** consists of **two neutrons and two protons** — **the same as a helium nucleus**. It is comparatively large and heavy, and carries a charge of +2.

**Beta (β)** is **a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton**. Note where it comes from: the **nucleus**, not the electron shells, and it exists only because a neutron has changed into a proton.

**Gamma (γ)** is **electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus**. It has no mass and no charge.

**A neutron (n)** may also be emitted.

**The specification limits what you need** to three properties: **penetration through materials**, **range in air**, and **ionising power**. Nothing else about them is required.

**Alpha** is stopped by **paper or skin**, travels only **a few centimetres** in air, and is the **most ionising**.

**Beta** is stopped by **a few millimetres of aluminium**, travels about **a metre** in air, and is **moderately ionising**.

**Gamma** is reduced by **thick lead or concrete**, travels a **very long way** in air, and is the **least ionising**.

**The pattern, and the reason behind it.** Penetration and ionising power run in **opposite directions**. An alpha particle is highly ionising precisely **because** it interacts strongly with the atoms it passes — so it loses its energy quickly and cannot get far. Gamma interacts weakly, so it ionises little and travels a long way. One mechanism explains both columns.

steps.title: Nuclear equations
steps.body:
**Nuclear equations are used to represent radioactive decay**, and the emission of radiation **may cause a change in the mass and/or the charge of the nucleus**.

**Alpha decay** removes two protons and two neutrons, so it **decreases both the mass and the charge** of the nucleus: the mass number falls by **4** and the atomic number by **2**.

**Beta decay** does **not change the mass** of the nucleus but **increases its charge**. A neutron turns into a proton, so the total of protons and neutrons is unchanged — the mass number stays the **same** — while the atomic number rises by **1**.

**Gamma emission does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.** It carries away energy only.

**A worked alpha decay.** A nucleus of mass number 238 and atomic number 92 emits an alpha particle. The alpha takes away mass 4 and charge 2, so the nucleus left behind has:

- mass number $238 - 4 = $ **234**
- atomic number $92 - 2 = $ **90**

**Check by balancing**: $234 + 4 = 238$ ✓ and $90 + 2 = 92$ ✓. The two sides must agree on both numbers.

**Two things the specification says you do not need.** You are **not required to recall** the example decays. And balancing is **limited to the atomic numbers and mass numbers** — **the identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required**. So you never need to look up which element you have produced.

steps.title: Half-life
steps.body:
**The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve** — or, equivalently, **the time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample to fall to half its initial level**.

Both definitions are in the specification, and either earns the mark.

steps.title: Contamination, irradiation and background
steps.body:
**These two are constantly confused, and the difference is examined directly.**

**Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials.** **The hazard from contamination is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms**, and **the type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard**.

**Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation.** Crucially: **the irradiated object does not become radioactive.**

**So the difference is whether the radioactive atoms are present.** Contamination puts them **on or in** the object, so it keeps emitting until they are removed — and it may be very hard to remove them. Irradiation merely **shines radiation at** the object; once the source is taken away or shielded, the exposure stops.

**Which is worse depends on where you are.** **Contamination inside the body** is especially dangerous for **alpha**, which is the most ionising and would otherwise be stopped by skin — inside, there is no skin between it and living tissue. **Irradiation from outside** is more dangerous for **gamma**, which penetrates far enough to reach organs.

**Peer review.** The specification asks you to understand that **it is important for the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans to be published and shared with other scientists so that the findings can be checked by peer review.** Checking by other scientists is what makes the conclusions trustworthy.

**Background radiation is around us all of the time.** It comes from **natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space**, and **man-made sources such as fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents**. The level of background radiation and **radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location**. Dose is measured in **sieverts**, where 1000 millisieverts = 1 sievert — though **you do not need to recall the unit**.

steps.title: Uses, fission and fusion
steps.body:
**Nuclear radiations are used in medicine** for the **exploration of internal organs** and for the **control or destruction of unwanted tissue**.

**Exploring internal organs** uses a tracer: an isotope is given to the patient and a detector outside the body follows where it goes. This needs radiation that **escapes the body** — so **gamma** — and a **short half-life**, so the patient is not exposed for longer than necessary.

**Destroying unwanted tissue**, such as a tumour, uses radiation aimed to deposit energy where it is wanted. The judgement is always a **balance of risks**: the radiation is itself harmful, and the question is whether the harm it does is smaller than the harm of the untreated disease.

**Half-life changes the hazard.** Radioactive isotopes have a **very wide range of half-life values**. A **short** half-life means intense activity that **fades quickly**; a **long** half-life means weaker activity that **persists for a very long time**. Neither is simply safer — which is the point of the comparison.

**Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus**, such as uranium or plutonium. **Spontaneous fission is rare**: usually the unstable nucleus must **first absorb a neutron**.

The nucleus then **splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays**. **Energy is released**, and **all of the fission products have kinetic energy**.

**The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction.** In a **nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled** to control the energy released. **The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction** — the same physics, with nothing absorbing the spare neutrons.

**Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.** In this process **some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Separate activity from count-rate.** **Activity** is the rate at which the **source** decays, in **becquerel**. **Count-rate** is what a **detector records** each second. The count-rate is always **lower**, and it falls if the detector is moved away even though the activity is unchanged.

**Explain penetration and ionising power with one mechanism.** Alpha is **most ionising** because it interacts strongly with the atoms it passes — and that is **why** it loses energy quickly and is **least penetrating**. One cause, both columns. An answer that lists the properties without linking them has learnt a table rather than the physics.

**Say where a beta particle comes from.** It is **ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton** — not from the electron shells. That also explains why beta decay leaves the **mass number unchanged** while the **atomic number rises by 1**.

**Balance both numbers, and stop there.** Nuclear equations are **limited to balancing atomic and mass numbers**, and **identifying daughter elements is not required**. Reaching for a periodic table is time spent on something that carries no marks.

**Count the halvings first.** Time elapsed ÷ half-life, then halve that many times — or divide by $2^n$. The commonest error is treating halving as **subtracting** a fixed amount, which after 3 half-lives gives a badly wrong answer.

**Say that activity never reaches zero.** Each half-life removes half of **what remains**, not a fixed quantity. That is exactly why long-lived waste stays hazardous for so long.

**Be exact on contamination and irradiation.** The **irradiated object does not become radioactive**. Contamination means the radioactive **atoms are present**, so it continues until they are **removed**. And say which is worse **where**: alpha is most dangerous as **internal contamination**, gamma as **external irradiation** — because alpha cannot get through skin from outside, and gamma can.

**Justify a tracer's properties.** **Gamma**, so it escapes the body to reach the detector, and a **short half-life**, so the patient is not exposed longer than necessary. Both halves, with reasons.

**Keep fission and fusion apart precisely.** **Fission splits a large, unstable nucleus** after it **absorbs a neutron**, releasing **two or three neutrons** that may begin a **chain reaction** — **controlled** in a reactor, **uncontrolled** in a weapon. **Fusion joins two light nuclei**, and **some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation**.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Unstable nuclei emit radiation **to become more stable** — a **random** process.
- **Activity** is the rate a source decays, in **becquerel (Bq)**.
- **Count-rate** is decays recorded per second by a **detector**; always lower than activity.
- **Alpha**: two protons and two neutrons — a **helium nucleus**.
- **Beta**: a **high speed electron from the nucleus**, as a **neutron turns into a proton**.
- **Gamma**: **electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus**.
- Properties are limited to **penetration, range in air and ionising power**.
- **Alpha**: stopped by **paper**, a few cm in air, **most ionising**.
- **Beta**: stopped by **a few mm of aluminium**, about a metre, moderate.
- **Gamma**: reduced by **thick lead or concrete**, very long range, **least ionising**.
- **Alpha decay**: mass **−4**, atomic number **−2**. **Beta**: mass **unchanged**, atomic **+1**. **Gamma**: **neither changes**.
- **Half-life** is the time for the number of nuclei, or the count rate, to **halve**.
- **Contamination**: radioactive atoms **present**. **Irradiation**: the object **does not become radioactive**.
- **Fission**: a large unstable nucleus **absorbs a neutron** and **splits**, giving 2–3 neutrons and a possible **chain reaction**.
- **Fusion**: two **light** nuclei **join**; some mass becomes the **energy of radiation**.

questions.prompt: Describe the three types of nuclear radiation, comparing their penetration, range in air and ionising power, and explain why these properties are related.
questions.solution:
An **alpha particle (α)** consists of **two neutrons and two protons** — the same as a **helium nucleus**. It is relatively large and massive and carries a charge of +2.

A **beta particle (β)** is **a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton**. It is important that it comes from the **nucleus**, not from the electron shells, and that it exists because a neutron has changed into a proton.

A **gamma ray (γ)** is **electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus**. It has no mass and no charge.

**Penetration.** Alpha is stopped by **paper or skin**. Beta is stopped by **a few millimetres of aluminium**. Gamma is only **reduced** — not fully stopped — by **thick lead or concrete**.

**Range in air.** Alpha travels only **a few centimetres**; beta about **a metre**; gamma a **very long way**.

**Ionising power.** Alpha is the **most ionising**, beta **moderately** ionising, and gamma the **least ionising**.

**Why these properties are related** is the important part, because the two orderings run in **opposite directions** and that is not a coincidence — it is a single cause seen twice.

Ionising means knocking electrons off the atoms the radiation passes. An alpha particle is **large, slow-moving and doubly charged**, so it interacts **strongly** with almost every atom near its path, stripping electrons from a great many of them. That is what makes it **highly ionising**.

But each of those interactions **takes energy from the alpha particle**. Interacting with so many atoms means it loses its energy very rapidly, and once the energy is gone it stops. So the very property that makes it **strongly ionising** is what makes it **poorly penetrating** — it is stopped within a few centimetres of air.

Gamma sits at the other extreme. Having **no charge and no mass**, it interacts only **weakly** with the atoms it passes, so it ionises **little**. Losing energy slowly, it can travel a **long way** and pass through substantial thicknesses of material. Beta lies between the two on both counts.

So the rule to remember is that **ionising power and penetration are inversely related**, and the reason is that **ionising is how the radiation loses its energy**.

Explains why ionising power and penetration are linked.

questions.modelAnswer:
An **alpha particle (α)** consists of **two neutrons and two protons** — the same as a **helium nucleus**. It is relatively large and massive and carries a charge of +2.

A **beta particle (β)** is **a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton**. It is important that it comes from the **nucleus**, not from the electron shells, and that it exists because a neutron has changed into a proton.

A **gamma ray (γ)** is **electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus**. It has no mass and no charge.

**Penetration.** Alpha is stopped by **paper or skin**. Beta is stopped by **a few millimetres of aluminium**. Gamma is only **reduced** — not fully stopped — by **thick lead or concrete**.

**Range in air.** Alpha travels only **a few centimetres**; beta about **a metre**; gamma a **very long way**.

**Ionising power.** Alpha is the **most ionising**, beta **moderately** ionising, and gamma the **least ionising**.

**Why these properties are related** is the important part, because the two orderings run in **opposite directions** and that is not a coincidence — it is a single cause seen twice.

Ionising means knocking electrons off the atoms the radiation passes. An alpha particle is **large, slow-moving and doubly charged**, so it interacts **strongly** with almost every atom near its path, stripping electrons from a great many of them. That is what makes it **highly ionising**.

But each of those interactions **takes energy from the alpha particle**. Interacting with so many atoms means it loses its energy very rapidly, and once the energy is gone it stops. So the very property that makes it **strongly ionising** is what makes it **poorly penetrating** — it is stopped within a few centimetres of air.

Gamma sits at the other extreme. Having **no charge and no mass**, it interacts only **weakly** with the atoms it passes, so it ionises **little**. Losing energy slowly, it can travel a **long way** and pass through substantial thicknesses of material. Beta lies between the two on both counts.

So the rule to remember is that **ionising power and penetration are inversely related**, and the reason is that **ionising is how the radiation loses its energy**.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between radioactive contamination and irradiation, and evaluate which presents the greater hazard in different situations.
questions.solution:
**Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials.** The **hazard from contamination is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms**, and **the type of radiation they emit affects the level of hazard**.

**Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation.** The essential point, which the specification states directly, is that **the irradiated object does not become radioactive**.

**The difference is whether the radioactive atoms themselves are present.** In contamination they are **on or in** the object, so the object continues to emit radiation and will go on doing so **until the atoms are physically removed** — which may be extremely difficult, particularly if they are inside a body or absorbed into a porous surface. In irradiation, radiation has merely **passed through** the object; once the source is **removed or shielded**, the exposure stops immediately and nothing remains behind.

This is why food can be irradiated to kill bacteria and remain perfectly safe to eat: it was exposed to radiation, but no radioactive material was transferred to it.

**Which is the greater hazard depends on the situation, and particularly on the type of radiation.**

**For contamination inside the body, alpha is by far the most dangerous.** From outside, alpha is stopped by **skin** and does very little harm. But if an alpha-emitting substance is inhaled or swallowed, there is **no skin between it and living tissue**, and alpha's very high **ionising power** acts directly on cells, damaging DNA in a concentrated volume. A source that is nearly harmless in the hand becomes the worst case once inside.

**For irradiation from outside, gamma is the most dangerous.** Alpha cannot penetrate skin and beta only a little way, so neither reaches the organs. Gamma **penetrates deeply**, so an external gamma source can irradiate the whole body even at a distance, and shielding requires **thick lead or concrete**.

**So the ranking reverses depending on where the source is**, and a good answer says so explicitly rather than declaring one type simply "more dangerous". The practical consequences follow directly: workers handling alpha sources are protected mainly by preventing **ingestion and inhalation** — gloves, sealed sources, no eating in the laboratory — while protection from gamma sources is about **distance, time and shielding**.

**Contamination is generally the more serious problem overall**, because irradiation ends when the source is taken away while contamination persists, spreads, and may be impossible to clean up completely. That is why a nuclear accident releasing radioactive material is far more consequential than an equivalent exposure from a sealed source.

Finally, the specification notes that findings from studies into the **effects of radiation on humans should be published and shared** so they can be **checked by peer review** — because conclusions about hazards of this seriousness need independent scrutiny before they are relied upon.

examTechnique.body:
Keep **activity** (the source, in Bq) apart from **count-rate** (what a detector records). Link **ionising power** and **penetration** through one cause: strong interaction ionises and drains energy.

For half-life, **count the halvings first**. Remember the **irradiated object does not become radioactive**, and that balancing equations needs **no daughter element**.
examinerErrors: Using activity and count-rate as if they were the same.
Listing radiation properties without linking ionising power to penetration.
Saying a beta particle comes from the electron shells.
Trying to name the daughter element, which is not required.
Subtracting a fixed amount instead of halving for half-life.
Saying an irradiated object becomes radioactive.
Calling alpha "least dangerous" without saying from where.
Omitting that a nucleus usually absorbs a neutron before fission.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer distinguishes **activity** from **count-rate** and explains why the count-rate is lower. It links **ionising power** and **penetration** to a **single mechanism** rather than listing them, and places a beta particle firmly in the **nucleus**, as a **neutron becoming a proton**. It counts **halvings** and notes that activity **never reaches zero**, because each half-life removes half of **what remains**. On hazards it refuses the simple ranking: **alpha** is worst as **internal contamination**, **gamma** worst as **external irradiation**, and it explains why the order reverses. It knows fission needs a **neutron absorbed** first, and that a reactor and a weapon differ only in whether the chain reaction is **controlled**.
